content: Lichen nitidus is a chronic inflammatory skin condition of unknown cause. It is characterized by the presence of small, discrete, uniform papules measuring 1-2 mm in diameter. These papules are shiny, flat-topped, and can appear pale flesh-colored or reddish-brown. In individuals with darker skin tones, the papules may be hypopigmented. Occasionally, minimal scaling may be observed or induced by rubbing the surface of the lesions. This condition predominantly affects children and young adults. It is typically painless and non-itchy, although prolonged pruritus may occur in some cases. The papules often appear in linear arrangements, a phenomenon known as the Koebner phenomenon, particularly on the forearms. In some cases, the papules may be grouped but do not merge into larger lesions. They are commonly found in flexural areas. In more extensive cases, the papules may become widespread, appearing on various parts of the body, including the extensor surfaces of the elbows, wrists, and hands, as well as the neck folds, submammary regions in females, groin, thighs, ankles, and feet. These lesions may coalesce into erythematous plaques with minimal scaling. Over time, the redness of the plaques may develop hues of violet, brown, and yellow. Diagnosis of lichen nitidus is primarily clinical, based on the characteristic appearance of the skin lesions. The condition is often documented in dermatology atlases for reference. Treatment is generally not required, as lichen nitidus is asymptomatic and self-limiting in most cases. However, topical glucocorticoids may be used if treatment is desired. In cases where the disease is symptomatic, generalized, or extensive, oral glucocorticoids may be considered. Other reported treatment options include PUVA therapy, UVA/UVB phototherapy, astemizole, acitretin, and etretinate. Narrow-band UVB phototherapy has also been reported as an effective treatment in some cases.
